title: Six days of making (Genesis 1:6–31)
hook: sky, sea, land, lights, creatures, each day closing "and it was good"

segments.voice: Yesterday: Bereshit, in the beginning. God spoke, and light answered. Your line was words make worlds.

An empty apartment fills up in a certain order. First the rooms: walls, a floor, a window that lets the light in. Then what fills them: a lamp in the corner, fish in a tank, a cat on the sill, people around a table. Nobody hangs a picture before there's a wall. The first chapter of Genesis is built a lot like that apartment.
screen: `AN EMPTY APARTMENT.` → `FIRST THE ROOMS.` → `THEN WHAT FILLS THEM.`

segments.voice: Here are the six days. One: light, separated from dark. Two: a dome of sky, between the waters above and the waters below. Three: dry land, and plants growing on it. Four: the sun, the moon and the stars. Five: fish in the sea and birds in the sky. Six: animals on the land, and then human beings. Some readers see a pattern. The first three days make spaces: day, sky and sea, land. The next three fill them, in the same order: lights, then fish and birds, then creatures of the land. Rooms, then furniture. Now a puzzle the rabbis loved: light on day one, but no sun until day four. So what was that first light? The Talmud says it was a special light, by which a person could see from one end of the world to the other, and God hid it away for the righteous in the time to come. The text never even names the sun and moon. It calls them the greater light and the lesser light, lamps set in the sky to do a job. And yom, the word for day? Jewish readers have disagreed about whether these are days of twenty-four hours; the chapter doesn't stop to say. What it does say, again and again, is that each thing is made "after its kind," fully itself. You met the refrain on day six: and it was good. Then, at the end of the sixth day, looking at everything together: "and, behold, it was very good."
screen: `THREE DAYS OF ROOMS.` · `THREE DAYS TO FILL THEM.` · `LIGHT BEFORE THE SUN.` · `EACH AFTER ITS KIND.` · then, large: `AND, BEHOLD, IT WAS VERY GOOD.`

segments.voice: Look around slowly and name six good things you can see, one for each day of making. Light, the sky or air through a window, something that grew, something that shines, something alive, and a person or a trace of one, like a photo or your own hands. Say each one quietly, then let the list sit.
Yom, the Hebrew word for day, and one the rabbis debated. Three days of rooms, three of filling them, and the good counted all the way through.
Your line: count the good. The chapter keeps that count right to the end. Day twenty-three, done.

howItsDone: Jews read the six days of creation in the first Torah portion each autumn, and in the daily morning prayers praise God who renews the work of creation every day.

chat.says: Is there any order to the six days of creation, or is it just a list?
options: Some see a pattern: three days make spaces, the next three fill them.
Humans come first, and everything else is made around them.
No order really; the sun and light both arrive on day one.
chat.meaning: Days one to three make spaces: day, sky and sea, land. Days four to six fill them in the same order.
